description: Narrows code.structure.json for docs/code/package-*.md, which is applied as well. The prose authority is docs/__meta__/code-package.md. The frontmatter fixes type, and the form of name and scope: a package document names a top-level import package, such as lorecraft or lorecraft_gen. The five sections open the document, in this order, with a tighter cap on Responsibility and Publication, which each state one thing; the Checklist follows as code.structure.json places it, and References follows, required here though optional in the corpus; an optional External References closes it. The token budget is tighter than the corpus one, since a package document is loaded beside the code specs for the code being written.

outline.description: One sentence stating what the package is for, followed by the one reason it changes.
examples:
Hold the toolkit users install: the commands, the checks and the model they run over. It changes when a command, a
check or a specification dialect changes.

outline.description: Whether the package is built and published, how it reaches its users or its environment, and what keeps it out of an artifact when it is private.
examples:
It is the only package built and published: the wheel and the source distribution hold it and nothing else, and the
release workflow publishes both.

outline.description: A table of which packages this one may import and which may import it, one row per neighbour, with the contract, the gate or the review that enforces the direction.
examples:
| Package | It may import this package | This package may import it | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lorecraft_gen` | Yes | No | An import-linter contract, run by `just check` |

outline.description: A bulleted list of the conditions a change must keep for the package to stay what it is, each verifiable against a diff: what it ships, imports, restates and configures.
examples:
- Nothing outside `src/lorecraft/` is built into the wheel.
- No module imports a private package.

outline.description: One to three Bad/Good pairs, Bad first: each Bad is code or configuration a plausible change puts into the wrong package, each Good the same intent placed correctly, written as a fabricated example.
examples:
```python
# ❌ Bad — the published package imports a generator: the generator ships in the wheel
from lorecraft_gen.schemas import main as write_schemas
```

```python
# ✅ Good — the generator is a module a recipe runs, and nothing published reaches it
```

outline.description: The architecture document the package's rules build on, as Foundation; principle-single-responsibility as Foundation; and the sibling package document, as Companion.
examples:
- [principle-single-responsibility](principle-single-responsibility.md) - Foundation: One reason to change
- [package-lorecraft-gen](package-lorecraft-gen.md) - Companion: The package that imports this one

outline.description: Links to the outside sources the package's packaging rests on, such as the documentation of the build backend.
